headline: A giant rodent lived in Thailand 34 million years ago

sources.title: "Giant rat" weighing 66 pounds once roamed Thailand, fossilized teeth reveal (CBS News)
Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago (ScienceDaily)
Giant, prehistoric rodent fossils discovered in southern Thailand (EurekAlert!)
A giant eocene ischyromyid from Southeast Asia reveals the early evolution of rodent gigantism (Scientific Reports)

chunks.text: In 2004, a government [[geologist]], a scientist who studies rocks, found a large, [[pale]] object in a [[coal mine]] in southern Thailand. It {{stood out}} against the dark coal. She first thought it was a piece of bone. Her [[supervisor]] told her it was a giant rat's tooth. A second tooth {{turned up}} the same day. Both were [[fossils]], the hardened [[remains]] of ancient animals.

verbs.correct: To be easy to see against something
verbs.wrong: To be carried to a lab far away
verbs.why: A red car stands out in a parking lot full of gray ones. Her bright yellow coat stands out in any crowd. In 2004, a pale tooth stood out against the dark coal in a mine in southern Thailand.

verbs.correct: To be found, often by chance
verbs.wrong: To become soft in warm water
verbs.why: Lost keys often turn up in an old coat pocket. Old family photos sometimes turn up when people clean the attic. A second tooth turned up in the Thai coal mine the same day.

chunks.text: For over 20 years, nobody could {{figure out}} exactly what kind of animal the teeth belonged to. Scientists from Thailand, France and Canada {{teamed up}} to study them [[in detail]]. The animal was a [[rodent]], an animal with long [[front teeth]], like a rat or a mouse. The size and shape of the teeth {{set them apart}} from all known rodents. It is a new [[species]], or kind of animal. Their study was published on November 4, 2026.

verbs.correct: To find the answer by thinking
verbs.wrong: To keep something in a safe place
verbs.why: Most kids figure out simple puzzles very quickly. My dad figures out most problems with his computer himself. For over 20 years, nobody could figure out exactly what kind of animal the two teeth belonged to.

verbs.wrong: To lose a fossil on a trip
verbs.why: Two neighbors team up to clean the park every spring. Local shops team up for a big sale each year. Scientists from Thailand, France and Canada teamed up to study the teeth in detail.

verbs.wrong: To wash a fossil with water
verbs.why: A friendly smile sets a good waiter apart. Fresh bread sets this bakery apart from the others. The size and shape of the two teeth set them apart from all known rodents.

chunks.text: The teeth {{go back}} about 34 million years. Scientists think the animal [[weighed]] about 66 pounds, or 30 kilograms. That is about [[half the weight]] of a large capybara, the biggest rodent alive today. A biology professor on the team {{pointed out}} that the weight is only a [[rough guess]]. With just two teeth, scientists cannot {{put together}} a [[full picture]] of the animal. How it looked, what it ate and how it [[behaved]] are still unknown.

verbs.correct: To have existed since a time long ago
verbs.wrong: To be painted a bright color
verbs.why: This old church goes back about 300 years. Their family bakery goes back to 1920. The two fossil teeth from southern Thailand go back about 34 million years.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To show anger about a decision
verbs.why: Doctors often point out that sleep is important for health. Store workers point out that the sale ends on Sunday. A biology professor on the team pointed out that the animal's weight is only a rough guess.

verbs.correct: To join facts to form one idea
verbs.wrong: To give a study a short name
verbs.why: Detectives put together the story from many small clues. Doctors put together a clear picture from tests and questions. With just two teeth, scientists cannot put together a full picture of the giant rodent.

chunks.text: It belonged to an early group of rodents that {{died out}} long ago. Most giant rodents {{came along}} much later, in South America. The team says rodents grew very large earlier than scientists thought. The find also suggests Southeast Asia was important in early rodent history. The team {{came up with}} a two-part name. The first part [[combines]] a Thai word for "giant" and a Greek word for "mouse." The second part [[honors]] a Thai princess who supports science.

verbs.wrong: To win a prize for science
verbs.why: Some old customs die out when young people leave a village. Some kinds of birds die out when their forests disappear. The animal belonged to an early group of rodents that died out long ago.

verbs.correct: To appear or start to exist
verbs.wrong: To be given a Thai name
verbs.why: New phones come along every year. Better medicines come along all the time. Most giant rodents came along much later than the Thai species, in South America.

verbs.correct: To invent a new idea or name
verbs.wrong: To sell a fossil to a museum
verbs.why: Good teachers come up with fun games for class. Parents come up with a name before the baby is born. The team came up with a two-part name for the new species.

mainIdea.s: Scientists named a new giant rodent from two old teeth found in a Thai coal mine. The animal lived about 34 million years ago, so rodents grew very large earlier than once believed.
mainIdea.why: The teeth belong to a new species that weighed about 66 pounds. Most giant rodents came along much later, in South America.

mainIdea.s: Workers in southern Thailand found a whole skeleton of a huge prehistoric rodent. Because the bones are complete, the team knows exactly how heavy it was and what food it ate.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the team found only two teeth. The weight is a rough guess, and scientists cannot put together a full picture of how it lived.

mainIdea.s: Farmers in Thailand say large wild rats are eating more of their rice than before. Officials plan to send traps and train local workers to protect the next harvest in the south.
mainIdea.why: This story is about fossil teeth from a coal mine. Their size and shape set them apart, and they belong to a giant rodent that lived about 34 million years ago.

tf.s: A pale tooth stood out against the dark coal in a mine in Thailand.
tf.why: The geologist found a large, pale object in a coal mine, and it was easy to see against the dark coal.

tf.s: Scientists named the new species soon after the teeth were found.
tf.why: For over 20 years, nobody could figure out exactly what kind of animal it was. The study came more than 20 years later.

tf.s: The teeth belong to a kind of rodent that nobody knew about before.
tf.why: Their size and shape set them apart from all known rodents, so they come from a new species.

tf.s: A scientist pointed out that the animal's weight is only a rough guess.
tf.why: A biology professor who worked on the study said the weight of about 66 pounds is not exact.

tf.s: Scientists have put together a full picture of how the animal lived.
tf.why: With just two teeth, scientists cannot put together a full picture. How it looked, ate and behaved is still unknown.

tf.s: Most giant rodents came along in Southeast Asia, not in South America.
tf.why: Most giant rodents came along much later, in South America. This find suggests Southeast Asia was important early on.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the giant rat from Thailand?
A giant rat? That [[makes my skin crawl]]. How big was it?
About 66 pounds, [[give or take]]. That's about half the weight of a big capybara.
Wow. How do they even know that?
They don't know for sure. A scientist {{pointed out}} that it's only [[a ballpark figure]].
So what did they find? A whole skeleton?
Just two teeth. A geologist found one in a coal mine in 2004. It {{stood out}} against the dark coal.
Did she know what it was?
[[At first glance]], she thought it was a piece of bone. Then a second tooth {{turned up}} the same day.
And it took twenty years to study them?
Pretty much. Nobody could {{figure out}} exactly what kind of animal it was. Then scientists from three countries {{teamed up}} and [[took a closer look]].
It's a new species. The size and shape of the teeth {{set them apart}} from every known rodent. And they {{go back}} about 34 million years.
So why is that such big news?
Most giant rodents {{came along}} much later, in South America. So rodents got big a lot earlier than people thought.
And did the team {{come up with}} a good name for it?
The first part means "giant mouse." The second part honors a Thai princess who supports science.
Giant mouse. I like it. I'm just glad it's not in my kitchen.

expressions.def: Used to say that a number is close but not exact

expressions.def: A number that is a rough guess, not an exact amount
ex: Can you give me a ballpark figure for the repairs?

expressions.def: Used to say how something seems when you first see it
ex: At first glance, the two paintings look the same.
At first glance, the job seemed easy.
The mechanic took a closer look and found the problem.
